body_md: Generics `<T>` write code once for many types: `fn first<T>(v: &[T]) -> &T`. Monomorphization generates specialized copies — zero-cost abstraction with static dispatch.
hook: Write once, work for every type — with zero runtime cost.

quiz.explain: Monomorphization emits a copy per concrete type.
options: Monomorphized: one copy per concrete type
Type-erased to a single boxed version
Resolved through runtime type reflection
Dispatched through a vtable on every call
quiz.q: How are generics compiled?

takeaway: Generics give reuse with static zero-cost codegen.
trap: Over-generic APIs bloat binaries; bound tightly.

body_md: A **trait** defines shared behavior: `trait Speak { fn hi(&self); }`. Implement with `impl Speak for Dog`. Default methods provide fallback logic implementors can override.
hook: Interfaces without inheritance — traits do it better.

quiz.explain: Traits declare behavior; impl provides it per type.
options: Inherit methods from a base struct
Define a trait and impl it per type
Add the methods to a shared mod block
Derive them with #[derive(Behavior)]
quiz.q: How do you share behavior across types?

takeaway: Traits define behavior; impls attach it to types.
trap: Forgetting impl block; trait alone does not attach behavior.

body_md: Bounds like `<T: Clone + Debug>` require capabilities. `where T: Display` clauses keep signatures readable. Compiler checks bounds at each use site.
hook: Generic but make it safe — bounds are the guardrails.

quiz.explain: Bounds constrain T to types with required traits.
options: Add a trait bound like <T: Clone>
Just call .clone(); it's checked later
Annotate the param with #[clone]
Wrap T in Box<Clone> to require it
quiz.q: How do you require Clone on generic T?

takeaway: Bound generics to the traits they actually use.
trap: Missing bound gives `method not found` error at use.

body_md: Derive `Clone`, `Copy`, `Debug`, `PartialEq` instead of hand-writing. `#[derive(Debug)]` unlocks `{:?}`. Custom types need explicit derives — nothing is automatic.
hook: #[derive] writes Clone, Debug and PartialEq impls for you

quiz.explain: derive auto-generates standard trait impls.
options: #[derive(Clone, Debug)] on the type
Every struct gets them automatically
Inherit them from a base struct
Call clone!() and debug!() macros
quiz.q: How do you get Clone and Debug quickly?

takeaway: Derive standard traits; hand-write only custom logic.
trap: Deriving Copy on heap types fails; Copy needs Clone + stack-only.

body_md: **Lifetimes** `'a` describe how long refs stay valid. `fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str` ties output to inputs. Elision covers most cases silently.
hook: Lifetimes like 'a just tell the compiler how long refs live

quiz.explain: Lifetimes prove output refs never outlive inputs.
options: How long a reference stays valid
When the GC frees a heap value
The memory address a reference holds
How long a thread may keep running
quiz.q: What do lifetimes describe?

takeaway: Lifetimes tie reference validity to owner scopes.
trap: Annotating everything; trust elision for single input/output.

body_md: Elision rules: each `&` input gets a lifetime; single input flows to output; `&self` flows to output in methods. Only complex signatures need explicit `'a`.
code:
fn first(v: &[i32]) -> Option<&i32> { v.first() }
// elided: fn first<'a>(v: &'a [i32]) -> Option<&'a i32>
hook: You already use lifetimes daily — the compiler just hides them.

quiz.explain: Elision fills in the common single-borrow cases; you annotate only when the output could come from more than one input.
options: Yes, on every function with a &
No, elision covers common cases
No, lifetimes are fully inferred
Only on methods that take &self
quiz.q: Must you always write lifetimes?

takeaway: Rely on elision; annotate only ambiguous cases.
trap: Two inputs + output ref needs explicit lifetimes; elision fails.

body_md: Structs holding refs need lifetimes: `struct H<'a> { s: &'a str }`. The struct cannot outlive its borrow. Owned `String` avoids lifetimes entirely.
hook: Putting a reference inside a struct? Now you owe the compiler an explanation.

quiz.explain: A struct holding a borrow must declare a lifetime param so it can't outlive the data it points to.
options: Declare a lifetime: struct H<'a>
Just write &str; it's inferred
Only &'static str fields are allowed
Use a raw pointer instead of &str
quiz.q: How does a struct hold a &str field?

takeaway: Borrowing structs carry lifetime params.
trap: Storing temp ref in struct fails; owned String sidesteps it.

body_md: **Closures** `|x| x + 1` capture environment. `Fn` borrows, `FnMut` mutates capture, `FnOnce` consumes. Pass with `impl Fn(i32) -> i32` or generic `F: Fn()`.
hook: Closures are functions that capture their surroundings

quiz.explain: Closures capture; plain fns cannot.
options: Closures capture env; fn items don't
fn items capture env; closures don't
Both capture variables from scope
They're identical apart from syntax
quiz.q: How do closures differ from plain fn items?

takeaway: Closures capture context; fns are standalone.
trap: Storing closure needs Box<dyn Fn>; each closure has unique type.

body_md: `move` closures take ownership of captures — required for `thread::spawn`. Without move, closure borrows and may outlive locals. Use move when crossing threads.
hook: Spawning a thread? Your closure needs the move keyword

quiz.explain: The thread may outlive the caller, so move transfers ownership of captures into it.
options: A move closure that owns its captures
A closure that borrows locals by &
Any closure, as long as it is Copy
A plain fn item, since closures can't
quiz.q: What closure does thread::spawn usually need?

takeaway: Use move closures to transfer ownership to threads.
trap: Forgetting move gives `may outlive borrowed value` error.

body_md: **Iterators** are lazy: `map`, `filter` build pipelines; `collect`, `sum` consume them. `v.iter()` borrows, `into_iter()` owns. Zero-cost — compiles to loops.
hook: Iterators are lazy: map and filter run only when consumed

quiz.explain: Adapters like map and filter are lazy; consumers like collect or sum drive the whole pipeline.
options: Immediately, each building a new Vec
Only when a consumer like sum runs
In a background thread as you chain
When the iterator variable is dropped
quiz.q: When do map/filter execute?

takeaway: Build lazy pipelines, terminate with collect or fold.
trap: Forgetting collect runs nothing; pipeline silently dropped.

body_md: `collect()` infers target via turbofish: `collect::<Vec<_>>()`. Use `sum`, `count`, `fold` for scalars. `partition` splits into two collections at once.
hook: collect() builds whatever collection you annotate

quiz.explain: collect builds any type implementing FromIterator; the annotation or turbofish picks which.
options: Only a Vec matching the item type
Any FromIterator type you annotate
Only Vec, HashMap, or HashSet types
Whatever type the iterator came from
quiz.q: What can collect() build?

takeaway: Annotate or turbofish collect targets explicitly.
trap: Missing type annotation gives `cannot infer type` error.

body_md: `impl Trait` in args accepts any impl: `fn f(x: impl Display)`. In return, it hides concrete type: `-> impl Iterator<Item=i32>`. One type only — not dynamic dispatch.
hook: Return a type without naming it — impl Trait is the trick.

quiz.explain: Return-position impl Trait hides one concrete type chosen by the function; dispatch stays static.
options: One concrete type, hidden from callers
Any iterator type, chosen at runtime
A boxed iterator with dynamic dispatch
The caller picks the iterator type
quiz.q: What does `-> impl Iterator` mean?

takeaway: impl Trait abstracts types statically.
trap: Returning two different impl types fails; use dyn or enum.

body_md: `Box<T>` owns heap data with single ownership. Use for recursion (`Box<Node>`) or large types. `Box::new(v)` allocates; deref with `*`.
hook: Infinite size error? One Box fixes recursive types.

quiz.explain: Box uniquely owns heap data and is pointer-sized, which is why it breaks infinite recursive types.
options: A garbage-collected pointer to heap data
A sole owner of heap data, fixed size
A reference-counted shared pointer
A stack slot that grows as T grows
quiz.q: What is Box<T>?

takeaway: Box enables recursion and heap ownership.
trap: Recursive enum without Box gives infinite-size error.

body_md: `Rc<T>` is **shared ownership** with refcount (single-threaded). `clone()` bumps count, last drop frees. Pair with `RefCell` for interior mutability.
hook: Rc gives one value many owners, on a single thread

quiz.explain: Rc::clone bumps a refcount instead of copying; the value is freed when the last Rc drops.
options: Rc: clones bump a reference count
Box: clone the box to share it
&mut: hand each owner a mutable ref
Copy: duplicate it into each owner
quiz.q: How can two owners share one value on a single thread?

takeaway: Rc shares ownership via reference counting.
trap: Rc cycles leak; break with Weak for parent pointers.

body_md: `RefCell<T>` moves borrow checks to **runtime**: `borrow()` shared, `borrow_mut()` exclusive. Panics on violation. Enables mutation through `&` (interior mutability).
hook: RefCell: mutate through a shared ref, checked at runtime

quiz.explain: RefCell tracks borrows at runtime; a conflicting borrow_mut panics instead of failing to compile.
options: At compile time, like normal references
At runtime, panicking on a conflict
It doesn't; it skips borrow checks
With a lock that blocks until free
quiz.q: How does RefCell check borrows?

takeaway: RefCell enables mutation behind shared refs.
trap: Double borrow_mut panics at runtime; scope borrows tightly.

body_md: Blanket impls auto-apply: `impl<T: Display> ToString for T`. Extension traits add methods to foreign types. Orphan rule: impl Trait for Type needs local trait or type.
hook: Extension traits add methods to types you did not write

quiz.explain: The orphan rule needs the trait or the type to be local; Display and Vec both come from std.
options: Yes, any trait for any type is fine
No, neither trait nor type is local
Yes, if you put it in a pub module
Yes, as long as T is a local type
quiz.q: Can you impl Display for Vec<T> in your crate?

takeaway: Orphan rule keeps trait coherence globally.
trap: Impling foreign trait for foreign type errors; wrap in newtype.

body_md: Default type params and associated types keep generics ergonomic: `trait Add<Rhs=Self>`. `type Output;` declares per-impl result type. Keeps call sites clean.
hook: Generics with outputs that change per type — associated types.

quiz.explain: Associated types let each impl pick its output.
options: A generic parameter: Iterator<T>
An associated type: type Item = ...
A lifetime parameter on next()
Inferred from the first next() call
quiz.q: How does each Iterator impl choose its Item type?

takeaway: Associated types customize trait outputs per impl.
trap: Confusing generic param vs associated type; assoc needs no annotation.

body_md: Sort with `sort_by_key`, dedupe, binary_search on sorted Vec. `chunks(n)` batches slices. Prefer iterator adapters over manual index loops for clarity.
hook: Sort plus dedup in two lines — collections done right.

quiz.explain: dedup only removes consecutive duplicates, so sort first to make equal items adjacent.
options: Call dedup() on it as-is
Call sort(), then dedup()
Call reverse(), then dedup()
Call sort_unstable() alone
quiz.q: How do you remove all duplicates from a Vec?

takeaway: Combine sort and dedup for uniqueness.
trap: Dedup without sort leaves non-adjacent dupes behind.

body_md: `Cow<'a, str>` is **clone-on-write**: borrows until mutation forces owned String. Perfect for functions that usually read but sometimes edit.
hook: Cow borrows by default and clones only when you write

quiz.explain: Cow borrows until write forces owned copy.
options: Borrows until a write forces a clone
Always clones input to stay safe
Copies the data on every read access
Counts owners like Rc and shares
quiz.q: What does Cow do?

takeaway: Cow defers cloning until mutation needs it.
trap: Matching Cow without * or as_ref compares enum, not content.

body_md: Write generic helpers with `AsRef<str>` / `AsRef<Path>` params to accept many types. `fn open<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P)` takes &str, String, PathBuf alike.
hook: AsRef lets one signature accept String, &str and PathBuf

quiz.explain: String and &str both implement AsRef<str>, so as_ref() yields a &str from either.
options: S: Copy, so both pass by value
S: AsRef<str>, then call .as_ref()
S: AsMut<str>, then call .as_mut()
S: Into<&str>, then call .into()
quiz.q: Which bound accepts &str and String together?

takeaway: Use AsRef bounds for flexible borrowed params.
trap: Taking String directly rejects &str callers needlessly.
